suggestions.assertion: No piece of the audit runs on haiku; the auditing model is sonnet or better because auth is risk 2
suggestions.reason: This bundles two claims into one pass/fail. A run that dispatches nothing at all would trivially satisfy the 'no haiku' half while giving no actual guarantee about audit quality. Splitting it into (a) no dispatched piece is haiku and (b) the run explicitly commits the auditing work to sonnet-or-better would grade the without-skill baseline more precisely -- in the paired without-skill run, the only model tier named anywhere in its document is Haiku (proposed for an un-dispatched verifier), which is a meaningfully weaker posture than this run's explicit sonnet floor for both audit and verify, but the current wording makes that distinction hard to score cleanly.

No assertion checks whether the audit itself ever actually gets executed and a findings report returned to the user. This run's outputs_dir contains only the routing decision and the decision log -- no audit report, per-handler findings table, or evidence that the described subagents actually ran. If the skill under test is meant to produce a completed audit (not just a routing plan), the assertion suite currently can't catch a run that writes an excellent dispatch plan and never carries it out.

The fixture contains a deliberate, easy-to-miss trap that a real audit and a real verifier would need to catch: app/routes/admin.py's set_tier handler sits under /admin and mutates a user's tier, but never calls require_admin in its body (only the sibling all_users handler does) -- exactly the 'confident false negative' the verifier assertion gestures at. No assertion actually checks whether this specific gap gets found, so the eval can't distinguish a plan that talks about catching false negatives from one that would actually catch this one.

suggestions.assertion: Sizes the repo (counts handlers or route modules) before choosing between fan-out and a single agent
suggestions.reason: Both runs in this pair satisfy this assertion and the fan-out-reasoning assertion regardless of whether the skill was loaded -- a reasonably careful agent does this without any special framework. These two assertions don't discriminate between the with-skill and without-skill conditions here and mostly measure general competence rather than the skill's specific contribution.

eval_feedback.overall: The three assertions that depend on the skill's specific machinery (explicit S/R/A/K/I/P/V scores, a genuinely independent dispatched verifier, and a decisions.jsonl log entry) are sharp and clearly discriminating -- they cleanly separated this run from its without-skill counterpart. The sizing and fan-out-reasoning assertions were satisfied by both runs and add less discriminating signal. The biggest structural gap is that no assertion verifies the audit was actually carried out or that its findings would be correct -- the suite currently grades the plan to audit, not the audit itself.
